Q: Merge rows of a SQL table to fill null with existing values A:

Having NULLs in a table, wherever they are, is the consequence of a bad database design.

In RDBMS, R denotes the notion of relational, that is to say, different mathematical objects containing information and interacting with each other.

In your case, a correct design would be :

CREATE TABLE A (A_ID INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE A_SUB (A_ID        INT NOT NULL REFERENCES SO_79956624.A (A_ID),
                    SUB_KEY     CHAR(1) NOT NULL,
                    SUB_VALUE   NVARCHAR(32) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
                    PRIMARY KEY (A_ID, SUB_KEY));

You can then create a view to tabulate the result and present it in a single table... Either using the PIVOT operator if your RDBMS supports it, otherwise using the CASE operator:

CREATE VIEW V_A 
AS
SELECT A.A_ID, CASE SUB_KEY WHEN 'A' THEN SUB_VALUE END AS A, 
       CASE SUB_KEY WHEN 'B' THEN SUB_VALUE END AS B 
FROM   A AS A
       JOIN A_SUB AS SA
          ON A.A_ID = SA.A_ID;

That give you exactly the primal form of your table :

INSERT INTO A VALUES (1);

INSERT INTO A_SUB
VALUES (1, 'A', 'value1'),
       (1, 'B', 'value2');

A_ID        A                                B
----------- -------------------------------- --------------------------------
1           value1                           NULL
1           NULL                             value2

Depending on your RDBMS, you can update the view's data, which will be reflected either directly in the underlying tables or indirectly using an INSTEAD OF trigger. As an example (Microsoft SQL Server) :

CREATE TRIGGER E_I_A
   ON A
   INSTEAD OF INSERT
AS

BEGIN

   INSERT INTO A
   SELECT DISTINCT A_ID
   FROM   inserted
   EXCEPT
   SELECT A_ID
   FROM   A;

   INSERT INTO A_SUB
   SELECT *
   FROM   inserted;

END;

NOTE : PostGreSQL neads a more complicated code to do the same thing and uses two objects (a function and the trigger) instead of a simple trigger. Help you with https://neon.com/postgresql/triggers/instead-of-triggers. Also PostGreSQL INSTEAD OF triggers ar not set based (they runs for EACH ROWS) which is less performant rather than set based triggers like SQL Server...

Thus you can inserts one or multiple rows into the sets of the two tables...

INSERT INTO V_A
VALUES (2, 'A', 'value3'),
       (2, 'B', 'value0');

Of course you have to create INSTEAD OF UPDATE and INSTEAD OF DELETE triggers.

The difficulty is to maintain the number of the columns of the view. This can be automatically programmed in the INSERT / UPDATE INSTEAD OF trigger. To know if a column exists or not in the view definition, you can use the SQL ISO standard view INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS :

SELECT DISTINCT SUB_KEY
FROM   inserted
EXCEPT
SELECT COLUMN_NAME
FROM   INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS
WHERE  TABLE_NAME = 'V_A'

Then pick the definition of the view from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS, column VIEW_DEFINITION, and add the definition of those new pseudo-columns just before of the FROM clause :

, 
       CASE SUB_KEY WHEN 'C' THEN SUB_VALUE END AS C,        
       CASE SUB_KEY WHEN 'D' THEN SUB_VALUE END AS D

Enjoy SQL !

Q: Should trailing slash URLs redirect to non-trailing slash URLs? A:

Strictly speaking, /en/ is supposed to represent something like a directory listing (i.e. a collection of subresources), while /en should be a single resource. However, exploiting this small distinction in your application to an extent where it makes a functional difference would be an anti-pattern in itself.

Wasting traffic and compute (however small) with redirects just to stick to the convention has no benefits.
